Project Name: CapKey
Applicant: Terry Jn. (TeeYml on GitHub)
Funding Requested: $720 (paid in CKB, payout address provided upon approval)
Duration: 5 Weeks
License: MIT
Contact: Nervos Talk direct message
Ecosystem Alignment: AI Machine Payments, Browser Self-Custody Sessions (BSS)
Applicant Profile
Terry Jn. (TeeYml on GitHub) is an independent full-stack and web3 engineer with experience building smart contracts, transaction serialization pipelines and developer tooling across UTXO and account-based ecosystems.
GitHub: https://github.com/TeeYml
Repository: https://github.com/TeeYml/capkey
1. Executive Summary
CapKey is an on-chain covenant vault protocol and client SDK for Nervos CKB that lets wallet holders delegate strictly bounded spending power to temporary sub-keys.
In modern Web3 applications and autonomous agent pipelines, key management faces a sharp tradeoff between user friction and catastrophic key exposure. In browser dApps, requiring a wallet popup for every 5 CKB micro-action creates unbearable user fatigue in games, streaming payments and social tipping. Conversely, handing an unconstrained hot private key to an AI agent or browser local storage exposes the entire wallet balance to theft from a single prompt injection or malicious dependency.
CapKey solves this natively at the CKB consensus level. By locking funds into a capkey-lock Vault Cell, the master account owner defines non-bypassable constraints:
Per-Transaction Cap: A hard ceiling on how much can be spent in any individual transaction.
Cumulative Allowance: An exact step-down budget across the lifetime of the sub-key.
Single-Successor Rule: Exactly one vault Cell in and one out, so a spend cannot split or merge vaults to dodge the caps.
Sequence Counter: Each delegate spend raises last_sequence by one, giving verifiers an ordered history.
Owner Recovery: The owner can sweep or rotate the vault at any block.
Because CKB utilizes the UTXO Cell Model, these rules are enforced directly by recursive script covenants on the transaction outputs without requiring the heavy smart-contract account abstraction layers (ERC-4337) or centralized relayer infrastructure needed on account-based chains.
2. Motivation & Ecosystem Need
The Nervos Opportunity Map for AI, Machine Payments and Fiber in 2026 ( AI, machine payments, and Fiber in 2026: an opportunity map for CKB and Fiber developers ) designates Browser Self-Custody Sessions (BSS) as a high-priority track under “Validate Next”, highlighting two critical emerging use cases:
Enabling browser users to conduct repetitive on-chain interactions without signing continuous wallet popups.
Providing autonomous AI agents with scoped, bounded on-chain balances so they can pay for inference, data or tooling without access to the operator’s master treasury.
Why Existing Approaches Fall Short
Approach

Cold wallet signs every micro-action

Defeats self-custody; requires user trust and creates regulatory counterparty risk
EVM Account Abstraction (ERC-4337)
Smart-contract wallet with session keys
Extreme complexity; requires user-ops, bundlers, paymasters and high gas overhead
CapKey provides a native CKB answer: a lightweight, recursive covenant lock script where every sub-key spend is validated directly by CKB-VM nodes.
3. Protocol Architecture & Invariants
CapKey operates via a hierarchical key model: the Cold Master Key retains unconstrained ownership, while the Hot Delegate Key holds covenant-restricted spending permissions.
Vault Transition Flow
Input vault Cell (500 CKB, allowance 250, max_per_tx 100, seq 0)
+ input locked by delegate_lock_hash (its lock checks the signature)
|
v
Output 0: successor vault Cell (420 CKB, allowance 170, max_per_tx 100, seq 1)
Output 1: recipient Cell (79.99 CKB)
80 CKB left the vault: 79.99 to the recipient and 0.01 as fee
Binary Cell Layout (CK01)
Lock Script Arguments (args) (64 bytes)
owner_lock_hash (32 bytes): lock hash of the owner wallet.
delegate_lock_hash (32 bytes): lock hash of the delegate key. Any CKB lock can fill this role.
Cell Data (28 bytes)
magic (4 bytes): ASCII identifier CK01.
max_per_tx (8 bytes, u64 LE): maximum shannons that may leave the vault in one transaction.
remaining_allowance (8 bytes, u64 LE): cumulative shannons the delegate may still spend.
last_sequence (8 bytes, u64 LE): counter raised by one on each delegate spend.
Design choice: the delegate’s own lock checks the signature
The delegate path requires an input in the same transaction locked by delegate_lock_hash. That lock verifies the signature over the whole transaction, so capkey-lock contains no signature code. This keeps the script at 27 KB and lets the delegate be secp256k1, a WebAuthn lock such as JoyID or any other lock already on CKB.
Consensus Rules
Owner path: an input locked by owner_lock_hash is present. The script accepts.
Delegate path: an input locked by delegate_lock_hash is present and all of these hold:
One vault Cell is consumed and exactly one is created.
Output 0 carries the same capkey-lock script and no type script.
spent = input.capacity - output[0].capacity is above zero. It covers the recipient payment and the miner fee.
spent <= max_per_tx.
spent <= remaining_allowance.
Output 0 data keeps max_per_tx, lowers remaining_allowance by exactly spent and raises last_sequence by one.
Known limits
CKB has no upper bound on when a transaction may be committed so a lock cannot enforce “valid until time T”. CapKey does not claim expiry. The allowance bounds the loss and the owner can sweep at any time.
Caps apply to capacity only. xUDT and Spore assets are out of scope.
The recipient is not restricted.
4. Current State & Proof of Execution
The core lock already exists and is public, written in Rust and tested in the real CKB-VM:
Script: contracts/capkey-lock, ckb-std 1.1, no_std, 27,712 bytes.
Tests: 12 ckb-testtool tests. Each rejection test asserts the exact script error code.
Measured: 38,085 cycles for a delegate spend and 22,648 for an owner sweep, with an always-success delegate lock in the harness.
Reproduce: make test

5. Milestone Roadmap & Deliverables
The funded work runs for 5 weeks in four milestones.
Milestone 1: Real signature locks and testnet deployment (Week 1)
Add tests where the delegate is the secp256k1 sighash lock and where it is a WebAuthn (P-256) lock. Publish the cycle cost of each.
Add the cases missing from the current suite: a delegate input present but spending a different vault, two vaults in one transaction and u64 boundary values.
Deploy capkey-lock to CKB testnet and publish the code hash and deployment transaction.
Deliverable: tag v0.2.0.
Milestone 2: TypeScript SDK and CLI (Weeks 2-3)
@capkey/sdk on CCC with builders for vault creation, delegate spend, chained unconfirmed spends (up to 3) and owner sweep.
capkey issue and capkey pay working against testnet.
Deliverable: published npm package and CLI.
Milestone 3: Public web app (Week 4)
Connect a testnet wallet, fund a vault and issue a delegate key.
The delegate key is a WebCrypto key with extractable: false stored in IndexedDB, so page scripts can sign but cannot export it.
A demo store spends from the vault with no wallet popups and shows remaining_allowance falling.
A “Simulate Rogue Drain” button submits an over-cap transaction and shows the node’s script error.
Deliverable: live URL.
Milestone 4: Verifier, guide and video (Week 5)
capkey verify <tx_hash> rebuilds the input state, outputs and caps from CKB RPC and prints pass or fail.
Integration guide for dApps and AI agent frameworks.
Short walkthrough video.
Deliverable: verifier, guide, video and a closing report.
6. How to Verify
Every milestone includes self-contained reproduction commands requiring no subjective review:
Native Script Verification:
git clone https://github.com/TeeYml/capkey.git
cd capkey
make test
Every adversarial case fails inside the CKB script with its expected error code while valid transitions succeed.
Public Web Experience:
Navigate to the hosted testnet web app.
Connect JoyID or MetaMask, deposit 500 CKB and issue a 100 CKB sub-key with a 25 CKB per-tx limit.
Click “Purchase Item (10 CKB)” three times: payments confirm on testnet with zero wallet popups.
Click “Simulate Rogue Drain (150 CKB)”: transaction is rejected by CKB RPC.
Click “Revoke & Sweep”: master key reclaims all remaining vault funds to the cold wallet.
Independent RPC Verification:
npx capkey verify <tx_hash> --rpc https://testnet.ckbapp.dev/
Outputs parsed input vault parameters, deducted payment, fee breakdown, successor vault allowance and validation status.
On-Chain Explorer Verification:
Inspect published transaction hashes on pudge.explorer.nervos.org proving live deployment, delegate spends and master revocations.

recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project Overview
Project name: CKB Script Bench
One-sentence summary: An open, re-runnable test set of 24 CKB on-chain script tasks that measures whether AI-written lock and type scripts compile against the current ckb-std and hold up against malicious transactions, and whether CKB’s official AI resources fix the failures. A pilot on 3 tasks already found that the main failure is outdated or invented API use, not unsafe logic.
Project type: open-source benchmark (task set + hidden security tests + runner) and a public report, run in ckb-testtool / ckb-debugger. No chain deployment needed.
Funding requested: $980, paid in CKB
Duration: 6 weeks
CKB Script Bench is a measurement, not another AI assistant. It does not build a chatbot, a scaffold or an MCP server. It tests the ones that already exist and publishes where AI-written CKB scripts break.
2. Team Profile
Shobiye Abdulazeem (solo), backend / smart-contract engineer, Lagos, Nigeria].
I built Stellar tags, Human-readable payment tags for the Stellar network. Send to alice*stellartags instead of a 56-character G... address.
Has shipped on Stellar/Soroban.
Anything that breaks in ckb-testtool, ckb-debugger or the official docs gets written up and filed upstream.
GitHub: github.com/Abdulazeem-code · Repo: github.com/Abdulazeem-code/ckb-script-bench · Contact: Nervos Talk DM
3. Project Background
Why I want to build this. AI written ckb script was good, But it doesn’t seem safe for the developer and whatever product is being worked on And also Not all its code compile against the current ckb-std.
The gap this targets. CKB now officially recommends AI agents for script work. The docs publish llms.txt and llms-full.txt, list a community MCP server (CKB AI) and an agent skill (CKB Dev Skills), and ship a starter prompt to “Write, Test, and Deploy a CKB Script”. Nobody has published numbers on whether the scripts these agents write are safe.
An AI-written CKB script can fail in two ways. It may not compile against the current ckb-std, because the model learned an older API or invents methods. Or it compiles but is too permissive: a lock that ignores the script group, a token that doesn’t check overflow, or a timelock that reads since wrongly. The second is the expensive failure, so every task carries attack tests. The pilot below found the first is the common one today, and it is the one the official AI resources should fix.

None of the 8 answers was unsafe; every failure was API knowledge. 3 of the 4 answers to the Tier B brief failed to compile against ckb-std 1.1. Adding the official AGENTS.md fixed one of the two: it steered ChatGPT to real high_level functions, but it says nothing about what changed between ckb-std versions, so Gemini repeated its mistake.
This is one answer per model per condition: a signal, not a measurement. Prompts, unedited answers, compiler output and results are in the repo (run 01, run 02). The funded run repeats every cell with more tasks, models and runs.
4. Solution
What anyone gets (from week 5):
Clone the repo and run one command. It re-runs every hidden test against the published agent outputs, with no API keys needed.
Open the results page: pass rates per task, per model, per condition, and every unsafe script with the attack that broke it.
Optionally plug in your own model or agent setup and score it on the same 24 tasks.
The task set (24 tasks, Rust + ckb-std, as the official agent instructions recommend):
Tier
Tasks
Examples
A. Lock scripts
6 (2 built)
hash-preimage lock, owner lock by lock hash, absolute and relative timelocks via since, 2-of-3 multisig-lite
B. Type scripts
9 (1 built)
counter that only increments, simple token (output sum ≤ input sum unless owner mints), immutable data cell, one-time-unique cell (Type ID style)
C. Combined
9
escrow with refund after deadline, vault that must keep capacity, lock + type pairing, script reading cell deps
Each task has a plain-English spec (what an agent sees), 2–4 positive tests and 4–8 hidden attack tests (what it never sees). The attacks are the common CKB mistakes: extra inputs in the same script group, unchecked args length, outputs created without the type script, wrong since flags, sums checked on one side only.
Each task also has a brief: the interface only (args, cell data and witness format), the way a developer would ask. Scored runs use the brief, because in the pilot the full spec turned the safety rules into a checklist that every model followed. The set leans toward Tiers B and C because every Tier A answer in the pilot was correct; Tier A stays as a floor.
Conditions, each with the same prompt and the same three models (chosen at kickoff: two leading closed models and one open-weight model):
C0 bare model, no CKB context
C1 + AGENTS.md from ckb-script-templates (the pilot’s condition)
C2 + official llms-full.txt
C3 + CKB Dev Skills agent skill
The MCP server condition is left to ckb-ai-bench so the two projects do not overlap.

Duration: 6 weeks

2. Team Profile

Shobiye Abdulazeem (solo), backend / smart-contract engineer, Lagos, Nigeria].

An AI-written CKB script can fail in two ways. It may not compile against the current ckb-std, because the model learned an older API or invents methods. CKB Pulse started six weeks ago as one page that shows who is building on CKB, live. It has grown into something larger: a place where the work of every CKB builder is seen, credited, and turned into lessons the next builder can use. This post is what it does today.
VIDEO: Luso Crypto Labs on X: "Who's building on CKB right now? CKB Pulse shows it, live. And every fix a builder ships becomes a lesson for the next one: 198 so far, each linked to its commit. In your AI agent and on your pull requests. Free and open source. https://t.co/ICccqV4x2Q" / X
CKB Pulse, the live view1800×1125 249 KB
CKB Pulse
CKB Pulse
Pulse shows the public work of the CKB ecosystem as it happens, from GitHub: projects, people and updates in one place.
In short
Live. Every push, pull request, review, issue and release in the CKB projects on GitHub, as it happens. In the 30 days to 19 November: 5,514 updates by 213 people in 209 projects, not counting our own. Bots and AI agents are left out.
A new look. The whole site was redesigned, in dark and light, with a first page that says what it is.
Lessons from real fixes. 198 lessons so far, drawn from the public commits of 47 CKB projects. Each one is checked against the commit it came from and links to it.
Credit where the work was done. Every project has a card with who works on it and what CKB learned from it. Maintainers can confirm the lessons from their own project.
Inside your tools. An MCP server for AI agents, a check of your code against the lessons, and a GitHub Action that brings the lessons to your pull requests.
Free and open source (MIT), in English, 中文 and Português, on a phone or a computer.
A new look
The site was redesigned from top to bottom: straight corners, strong type, one red signal, and the name of who makes it under the title. The reading pages follow your device in dark or light, and you can switch. First-time visitors land on a page that says what Pulse is before the live view opens.
The weekly digest, dark and light1414×1480 275 KB
The address changed too: pulse.lusocryptolabs.com. Old links keep working.
What the ecosystem learned, kept for the next builder
Most of what builders learn on CKB stays in a commit message, or in nobody’s notes. Someone finds out that an absolute epoch since needs its flag, or that completeFeeBy adds a change output where they expected an output to shrink, fixes it, and moves on. The next builder hits the same wall.
Pulse reads the public commits of the projects it follows and keeps what they teach as short lessons: the rule, why it matters, the code before and after when the commit shows it, and the commit itself. A lesson is released only after it is checked against that commit and against the project’s code as it is today. A lesson that stops being true comes down.
A project card with its lessons, the lessons page, and a confirmed lesson2101×1480 684 KB
Browse and learn: CKB Pulse · What CKB learned, by topic and by level, with a start page, a glossary and a review mode.
Credit: every lesson names the project and links the commit. Every project card lists “What CKB learned from this project”.

recent_posts.content_text:
Hey @Fai !! Let’s continue here from the DAO thread.
DAO提案公平性疑问？
I’m really curious about how this massive project is doing after more than half a year?
Short version: the Rosen Team reviewed our design and found it sufficient, except for where Watchers and Guards read chain data. The integration is on hold on that point.
The full design is public in our tracker. While reviewing the Rosen code I also filed over 20 issues upstream.
The blocker: in their latest review they asked for at least three reliable public endpoints per network instead of requiring operators to run their own CKB nodes. This raised a red flag for me, which I shared in Nervos Nation and in the Rosen chat: each Guard checks deposits through one data source, by default a public RPC (Guards are the ones who jointly sign for the bridge funds).
In July someone tried to exploit the bridge with fake Cardano deposits. It failed only because the Guards happened to read different data sources, so not enough of them agreed. Nothing in the code makes them read different sources, on any chain. That’s why I opened this issue:
github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service
Enough Guards on one provider and a fake deposit pays out
opened 02:40PM - 13 Oct 26 UTC
phroi
Hi Rosen team,
I've been reading the Guard, Watcher, scanner and TSS code for t…he CKB integration for about a year. This is the most important thing I found, more than all the issues and private security reports I filed so far. It's not a bug in a function. It's a property the whole bridge relies on. Nothing in the code enforces it.
## The gap
In the [July security update](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63209) @zargarzadehm wrote for the team:
> The invalid events were successfully mitigated because guards operate on different independent data sources. Since Rosen requires consensus among guards, the attack was unable to satisfy the required quorum.
I agree, that's what saved it. My point: **this independence came from what each operator chose to configure, not from the code.** On `dev`:
- Each read goes to one configured network. For example, the [chain handler](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/src/handlers/chainHandler.ts#L119-L134) builds Ergo from the node or the explorer, never both.
- The shared [`verifyEvent`](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/packages/abstract-chain/lib/abstractChain.ts#L164-L259) reads the block transaction ids, the lock transaction and the block info from that one network. The Guard signs whatever that network answers.
- [`default.yaml`](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/config/default.yaml) ships public URLs that every Guard keeps unless the operator changes them, for example Blockstream for Bitcoin, Koios for Cardano, the Ergo Platform explorer for Ergo.
- A Guard doesn't tell the other Guards which source it reads, so nobody can see when quorum shares one provider.
So if enough Guards for quorum use the same provider, one wrong answer reaches all of them at once. Watchers on that provider report it, as the 84 invalid events in July show. Quorum then agrees on the same fake deposit. In July the attacker needed a scanner flaw to reach this. With a provider under their control, they don't. July was already close to this: Koios, the shipped Cardano default, was [the source returning the failed transactions](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63118). The Guards that rejected were the ones on another source. Had they kept the default too, quorum could have passed.
Every chain the Guard reads is affected. A fake deposit on any chain is paid from the custody of another.
You named this risk for Handshake. @mhssamadani, [in August](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63500):
> There are other minor reasons that slow down handshake however, one is the handshake has not enough data sources and this will be a point of failure that should be mitigated before going forward.
I'm asking the code to apply the same rule to the chains already live.
## Two boundaries I accept
No obligatory full nodes. @RaaCT0R was clear [in rcs#2](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/rcs/issues/2#issuecomment-5969120694):
> I don't think we can expect every Guard to run a full node on every network for Rosen, as that does not scale well.
Makes sense to me. Everything below works with public endpoints only.
No map of what Guards run. @Armeanio wrote two messages on [2 October](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/64436):
> I can’t claim what anyone runs on their computer with any level of confidence.
>
> If I had access to know that would be much less secure 🫡
Agreed on the second line. Direction 1 below tells the other Guards only which public provider a Guard reads per chain, with a self-hosted node shown as "own node". Direction 1 does give every Guard the list of providers the others read, so a compromised Guard learns it too. The shipped defaults already tell everyone the likely answer, but it is still the cost of making the property visible. Direction 3 shares nothing. And Guard-to-Guard traffic is [encrypted on the wire](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/rosenet/blob/488671348bab0c2fa48f238d74077b3801eee662/packages/rosenet-node/lib/createRoseNetNode.ts#L103), so none of it is visible to someone listening on the network.
**Choice is not a cross-check:** the [three endpoints rule](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/rcs/issues/2#issuecomment-5969120694) lets operators pick different sources, then switch when one is down. Neither picking nor switching catches a source that is up and gives a wrong answer. Only a second answer, compared before signing, does.
## Three directions, from cheapest to strongest
I sketched the first step of each against `dev` to see its shape (type-checked and unit-tested, never run against a network). I can share the diffs if useful.
### 1. Make it visible
Each Guard exposes which provider it reads per chain (or "own node") and shares that with the other Guards as an informational message. Each Guard can then raise a health alarm when one provider is close to the signing threshold. At this stage nothing is blocked. The property from the July update becomes checkable instead of assumed.
Rollout: an old Guard logs the message as an unexpected type and continues, so this can be released without a coordinated update, as long as the message is rare enough to not trigger the warn-log health check.
Second step: the same rule can block, no signing when the approving set reads one provider. That needs the tag inside the signed approval, so a coordinated update like the September audit fix. A chain with one provider then has no approving set that passes. Whether it stops until it has two, as Handshake needs before going forward in your words, or keeps running as exposed as today, is your decision. If it keeps running, the risk stays as today: a fake deposit there can be paid from any other chain's custody.
### 2. Say no explicitly
Today a Guard whose source disagrees [never answers](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/src/agreement/txAgreement.ts#L274-L281) the transaction request, so dissent looks like "not scanned yet". The rejected event's reason [is still a TODO](https://github.com/rosen-bridge/guard-service/blob/dc3be8cad8981e0248580c5dc04931a09e478e2d/services/guard-service/src/event/eventProcessor.ts#L66). Storing the real reason is the first small step. Then a reject answer with that reason, on the same channel, shows a disagreement immediately, instead of noticing it later like the [Bitcoin fee ratio case](https://t.me/rosenbridge_erg/63583) in August.
Non-agreement already pauses an event for a turn. A longer hold is the state question below.
### 3. Second source before signing
`verifyEvent` compares its three reads, plus the confirmation status, against a second configured source from a different provider, at the extracted-data level. It signs only when they agree. For most chains a second URL of the same network type is enough. A few extra calls per event, so free API tiers are enough. This is the one that verifies the answer: one poisoned provider can't get a signature from any Guard that enforces, whatever the other Guards chose. Once enough Guards enforce, the payout is blocked. It catches a provider answering wrong, not a bug shared by every client.
Rollout: shadow mode first. With no sources configured nothing changes. In shadow mode the only new behaviour is a log line and a health parameter. Then enforce per chain. A chain with one provider is the same call as in direction 1.
What these three miss stays bounded by cold storage as today: a bug shared by every client, or a one-provider chain if you keep it running.
The same check in the Watcher would help operators too: a Watcher reading a wrong source reports a false event, then its permits stay locked until a rescan or a Guard operator returns them, as after the July invalid events.
## From the sketches
All three are changes inside this repository only.
- A built network object doesn't know its own name or URL today, so for direction 1 the identity has to be recorded where the networks are built.
- Directions 2 and 3 share one design decision. Today an event is confirmed, rejected, or has no status yet, and the waiting statuses exist only after verification passed. An event blocked by a cross-check has nowhere to go. Whether such an event waits, expires or gets rejected is the question to settle first.
## What I'm asking
Which of these directions (or another rule) fits Rosen's architecture for Guards?
If a design review helps once you have something, ping me. Thanks for the quick fixes on #23 and #27!!
Keep up the Great Work,
Phroi
Rosen replied that a second source before signing costs too much in liveness and maintenance, so they are improving their anomaly detection instead. My concern: a provider that turns malicious can show a fake deposit only to the Watchers and Guards reading from it, while answering everyone else truthfully, anomaly detection included. Two weeks ago I followed up with a couple of questions and I’m still waiting for their answer.
My position: this is personal, not the one of Sonami (the DAO grant recipient). I cannot go ahead with the integration until this is solved on the Rosen side. What I suggested is at least one Guard that runs its own full node and can block a payout. I’d rather avoid another CKB bridge losing funds like Force Bridge.
DAO提案公平性疑问？
more than half a year
Delays on my side:
Lots happened in my personal life: we settled in a new country and had our first baby.
It took me a while to adopt LLMs, it only happened thanks to the Nervos Community Catalyst. At first I had OpenAI models and I was not happy with their code.
LLMs also make finding bugs in the code of others much cheaper. So I reviewed the Rosen codebase again and again until I could convince myself the CKB integration is safe.
Nowadays that’s mostly behind me: the baby is 7 months old and I switched to Claude for coding.
Delays on the Rosen side: they are a very competent team and I’m happy to work with them. Just their feedback can take months, even on crucial points: their answer on ACP and CKB state rent took about four months. My impression is that CKB is not their top priority. And their feedback decides whether the integration is done or thrown away, because they decide in the end.
DAO提案公平性疑问？
Why haven’t we seen any progress reports on it?
When there is something new, I post it here: dropping ACP, the full design and the Rosen review right above. Since October the main work has been this data-source issue.
Feel free to ask for an update anytime!
@Fai do you have any additional questions?
Love & Peace, Phroi

It signs only when they agree. For most chains a second URL of the same network type is enough. A few extra calls per event, so free API tiers are enough. This is the one that verifies the answer: one poisoned provider can't get a signature from any Guard that enforces, whatever the other Guards chose. Once enough Guards enforce, the payout is blocked. It catches a provider answering wrong, not a bug shared by every client. Rollout: shadow mode first. With no sources configured nothing changes. In shadow mode the only new behaviour is a log line and a health parameter. Then enforce per chain. A chain with one provider is the same call as in direction 1. What these three miss stays bounded by cold storage as today: a bug shared by every client, or a one-provider chain if you keep it running. The same check in the Watcher would help operators too: a Watcher reading a wrong source reports a false event, then its permits stay locked until a rescan or a Guard operator returns them, as after the July invalid events. ## From the sketches All three are changes inside this repository only. - A built network object doesn't know its own name or URL today, so for direction 1 the identity has to be recorded where the networks are built. - Directions 2 and 3 share one design decision. Today an event is confirmed, rejected, or has no status yet, and the waiting statuses exist only after verification passed. An event blocked by a cross-check has nowhere to go. Whether such an event waits, expires or gets rejected is the question to settle first. ## What I'm asking Which of these directions (or another rule) fits Rosen's architecture for Guards? If a design review helps once you have something, ping me. Thanks for the quick fixes on #23 and #27!! Keep up the Great Work, Phroi

Rosen replied that a second source before signing costs too much in liveness and maintenance, so they are improving their anomaly detection instead. My concern: a provider that turns malicious can show a fake deposit only to the Watchers and Guards reading from it, while answering everyone else truthfully, anomaly detection included. Two weeks ago I followed up with a couple of questions and I’m still waiting for their answer.

My position: this is personal, not the one of Sonami (the DAO grant recipient). I cannot go ahead with the integration until this is solved on the Rosen side. What I suggested is at least one Guard that runs its own full node and can block a payout. I’d rather avoid another CKB bridge losing funds like Force Bridge.

DAO提案公平性疑问？

more than half a year

Delays on my side:

  • Lots happened in my personal life: we settled in a new country and had our first baby.
  • It took me a while to adopt LLMs, it only happened thanks to the Nervos Community Catalyst. At first I had OpenAI models and I was not happy with their code.
  • LLMs also make finding bugs in the code of others much cheaper. So I reviewed the Rosen codebase again and again until I could convince myself the CKB integration is safe.

Nowadays that’s mostly behind me: the baby is 7 months old and I switched to Claude for coding.

Delays on the Rosen side: they are a very competent team and I’m happy to work with them. Just their feedback can take months, even on crucial points: their answer on ACP and CKB state rent took about four months. My impression is that CKB is not their top priority. And their feedback decides whether the integration is done or thrown away, because they decide in the end.

按照目前Community Fund DAO的规则，资助类提案如果有申请initial fund，那么在投票通过后，会由委员会进行打款。而后续里程碑支付则是按照项目提交Milestone 报告，依照以下规则，由社区进行审阅、提出问题。
CKB Community Fund DAO Rules and Process
社区成员也有权监督申请团队的工作成效和资金使用情况，并在论坛中发表评论或进行讨论。
若里程碑报告提交后一段时间，社区没有更多意见后，委员会会进行里程碑款项的支付。因为现行规则中对于社区审阅的时长没有明确声明，所以在实践中社区审阅期按照2周进行，即里程碑报告提交后，若社区没有更多意见的时间达到2周，委员会会进行打款。
不可否认的是，现行规则有非常多改善的空间，期待大家的更多讨论、治理实践，乃至发起元规则提案。

recent_posts.content_text:
Question for anyone thinking about reputation on CKB, since CrowdCell is about to start issuing crowdcell.campaign-funded.v1 claims through Vellum. Right now a funded-campaign badge is easy to fake: create a campaign, back it from your own wallet (or from as many fresh wallets as you like), hit the goal, get the money back on payout, and you’ve got the badge for a few tx fees. Something like “at least one backer who isn’t the creator” doesn’t fix it, since new wallets are free.
One idea is for the claim to carry the facts instead of a yes/no, and let readers and apps decide what they’re worth: number of distinct backer wallets, total raised, and how old the backer wallets were when they pledged. 40 backers with year-old wallets reads very differently from 5 wallets made the same day.
How would you game that, and what would you add or drop? I’m holding off on turning claims on until this is sorted. @truthixify curious what you think too, especially if Vellum already has a way to handle claims that carry evidence like this.

recent_posts.topic_title: CKB Mixer(混币器)——Tornado Cash on CKb
recent_posts.author: tianlitao
recent_posts.content_text:
过去一段时间用AI做了一个小项目，现在整条链路已经在 CKB 公共测试网上跑通了，发出来给有兴趣的人看。
一句话：用 Groth16 + Poseidon Merkle 树在 CKB 上实现了「存款 → 零知识证明 → 匿名取款」，所有验证逻辑写在真实的 CKB-VM 脚本里，能上链、能取钱；另外做了一个存款意向 + 聚合者的 v2，以及一个浏览器里就能用的网页 demo。
代码：https://github.com/tianlitao/ckb-mixer
线上 demo（仅测试网）：https://ckb-mixer.nervosscan.com/
为什么这件事在 CKB 上值得单独做一遍
Tornado Cash 在 EVM 上靠合约存储「这张 commitment 已经用过了」，CKB 的 cell 模型没有便宜的链上 map。但反过来，CKB 给了两个在 EVM 上不可能的结构性好处：
链上不需要存 Merkle 树。 池子 cell 里只有 1,640 字节状态：30 个历史根、20 层 frontier、nullifier 集合的根。树由脚本按 frontier 增量维护，存款时约 20 次 Poseidon。

代价也很 CKB：所有池子共用一个 cell，任何存款/取款都得花它。Tornado 的每笔交易独立、可并行；这里是个单点。这正是 v2 要解决的问题（通过聚合器和意图cell）。

FidelCoder – Blockchain Educator & Developer
FidelCoder is a distinguished blockchain expert and community leader in Africa, renowned for designing scalable decentralized systems. As an educator, he excels at demystifying complex blockchain concepts, guiding learners through building protocols and decentralized applications (DApps) with clarity and precision. Summary
Umojaverse is an Africa-focused builder community that brings blockchain, web3 and general tech together from the grassroots and across borders, so people learn and build products of real value. Through campus tours, ideathons, workshops and hackerhouses, it takes people from first curiosity to working prototypes.
The CKB Productathon is a competitive programme in Kenya that turns builders into teams with live products on CKB mainnet. It runs in two parts. The first is virtual: expert-led training on CKB technology and on building a startup, while teams ship and gather real users. The second is a two-day physical hackerhouse on the shore of Lake Victoria, where teams that have gone live build, demo and pitch for prizes. CellScript 0.33: Bounded Runtime Data and Stronger Artifact Checks
CellScript 0.33.0 is now released following two alpha releases.
My previous update covered 0.31’s work on executable size, argument decoding, and stack usage. The main work in 0.33 moves further into the language: bounded temporary collections, structured data, and checks that connect source-level operations to the generated artifact.
The stable release also fixes all four findings reported by an independent security review of the changes from 0.31.0 to 0.33.0-alpha.2.
Bounded temporary collections
Contracts can now use bounded temporary Vec, OrderedMap, and OrderedSet workspaces.
These collections have explicit resource limits and share a checked budget. This makes it possible to express temporary processing over transaction data while keeping its memory requirements bounded.
One detail matters when choosing those limits: the temporary arena is monotonic. Replacing or retiring a buffer does not immediately return its space to the budget; that space remains charged until the owning scope ends. Likewise, several collections can each satisfy their own item limit while exceeding their shared budget together.
The release includes copied reads, read-only helpers, and budget explanations. General heap reuse, mutable member loans, and escaping nested values remain outside the supported profile.
Structured data and Cell relationships
0.33 adds named bounded byte and record shapes, canonical codecs, non-escaping views, and checked Cell successors.
It also adds named heterogeneous Cell roles, bounded selection, and correspondence checks. These let a contract describe different participating Cells and check how they relate across a transaction, with source and schema authority retained through the supported paths.
The distinction between implemented and reserved forms remains explicit. ExactCellSelection is still reserved, and the broader representation and Cell-selection work continues under #96. Unbounded vectors with non-fixed elements remain outside the admitted codec.
Edition 2027 is now the source contract
Edition 2027 is the sole source edition across native compilation, packages, language services, and browser metadata compilation.
Ordinary actions, locks, lifecycle operations, and explicit or omitted verification use a shared checked grammar. Native type_script and lock_script containers retain their documented authoring limits.
The artifact formats have also moved forward. The current bundle uses metadata 75, lowering records v12, typed semantics v12, semantic foundation v4, and package interface v6.
For users, the practical consequence is to rebuild related outputs together. Metadata, lowering records, source maps, interfaces, and generated builders should come from the matching compiler and checker. Source edition, compiler version, artifact schema, and witness ABI remain separate identities.
Stronger independent artifact checks
The compiler now records structured effect facts for context reads, Cell lifecycle operations, and process operations. The standalone artifact checker reconstructs those facts independently from typed operations and callees.
Machine-code admission also checks more of the runtime boundary: PIPE success paths, SPAWN status guards, return conventions, ELF layout, and return-address slots.
This work strengthens the connection between the recorded operation and the executable being admitted. Its scope remains specific: structural validation and finite VM tests do not prove arbitrary source-to-machine equivalence.
The language server also uses captured, manifest-aware inputs for diagnostics and semantic hover, including unsaved package files and imports. Revision checks prevent an older analysis from publishing over newer edits, and invalid package manifests cannot obtain successful semantic metadata through a standalone fallback.
Four security-review fixes
Guopeng’s review reported one medium-severity finding and three low-severity findings. All four are fixed, with focused regressions:
Compiler resource amplification. A compact source could trigger a large aggregate expansion before resource checks ran. Type checking now enforces per-aggregate and cumulative module budgets before expansion, including native, metadata-only, LSP, and browser paths.
ZK request lifetime. The checker now rejects writes that could change initialized request words before transmission completes.
Certified fixed-field copies. Every certified frame copy now requires the exact bounded copy sequence whose stores stay within the certified destination.
Registry snapshot reservations. A rejected publication can no longer leave a tombstoned content hash permanently blocking another namespace’s legitimate publication. Active unverified admissions retain their conflict protection.
Relative to alpha.2, the stable release contains these fixes without changing the language surface, artifact schemas, metadata identities, or public APIs.
Updating a project
For an exact compiler pin, use this in each participating Cell.toml:
[package]
edition = "2027"
cellscript_version = "=0.33.0"

CellScript 0.33.0 is now released following two alpha releases.

My previous update covered 0.31’s work on executable size, argument decoding, and stack usage. The main work in 0.33 moves further into the language: bounded temporary collections, structured data, and checks that connect source-level operations to the generated artifact.

The stable release also fixes all four findings reported by an independent security review of the changes from 0.31.0 to 0.33.0-alpha.2.

Bounded temporary collections

Contracts can now use bounded temporary Vec, OrderedMap, and OrderedSet workspaces.

These collections have explicit resource limits and share a checked budget. This makes it possible to express temporary processing over transaction data while keeping its memory requirements bounded.

One detail matters when choosing those limits: the temporary arena is monotonic. Replacing or retiring a buffer does not immediately return its space to the budget; that space remains charged until the owning scope ends. Likewise, several collections can each satisfy their own item limit while exceeding their shared budget together.

The release includes copied reads, read-only helpers, and budget explanations. General heap reuse, mutable member loans, and escaping nested values remain outside the supported profile.

Structured data and Cell relationships

0.33 adds named bounded byte and record shapes, canonical codecs, non-escaping views, and checked Cell successors.

It also adds named heterogeneous Cell roles, bounded selection, and correspondence checks. These let a contract describe different participating Cells and check how they relate across a transaction, with source and schema authority retained through the supported paths.

The distinction between implemented and reserved forms remains explicit. ExactCellSelection is still reserved, and the broader representation and Cell-selection work continues under #96. Unbounded vectors with non-fixed elements remain outside the admitted codec.

Edition 2027 is now the source contract

Edition 2027 is the sole source edition across native compilation, packages, language services, and browser metadata compilation.

Ordinary actions, locks, lifecycle operations, and explicit or omitted verification use a shared checked grammar. Native type_script and lock_script containers retain their documented authoring limits.

The artifact formats have also moved forward. The current bundle uses metadata 75, lowering records v12, typed semantics v12, semantic foundation v4, and package interface v6.

For users, the practical consequence is to rebuild related outputs together. Metadata, lowering records, source maps, interfaces, and generated builders should come from the matching compiler and checker. Source edition, compiler version, artifact schema, and witness ABI remain separate identities.

Stronger independent artifact checks

The compiler now records structured effect facts for context reads, Cell lifecycle operations, and process operations. The standalone artifact checker reconstructs those facts independently from typed operations and callees.

Machine-code admission also checks more of the runtime boundary: PIPE success paths, SPAWN status guards, return conventions, ELF layout, and return-address slots.

This work strengthens the connection between the recorded operation and the executable being admitted. Its scope remains specific: structural validation and finite VM tests do not prove arbitrary source-to-machine equivalence.

The language server also uses captured, manifest-aware inputs for diagnostics and semantic hover, including unsaved package files and imports. Revision checks prevent an older analysis from publishing over newer edits, and invalid package manifests cannot obtain successful semantic metadata through a standalone fallback.

Four security-review fixes

Guopeng’s review reported one medium-severity finding and three low-severity findings. All four are fixed, with focused regressions:

  • Compiler resource amplification. A compact source could trigger a large aggregate expansion before resource checks ran. Type checking now enforces per-aggregate and cumulative module budgets before expansion, including native, metadata-only, LSP, and browser paths.
  • ZK request lifetime. The checker now rejects writes that could change initialized request words before transmission completes.
  • Certified fixed-field copies. Every certified frame copy now requires the exact bounded copy sequence whose stores stay within the certified destination.
  • Registry snapshot reservations. A rejected publication can no longer leave a tombstoned content hash permanently blocking another namespace’s legitimate publication. Active unverified admissions retain their conflict protection.

Relative to alpha.2, the stable release contains these fixes without changing the language surface, artifact schemas, metadata identities, or public APIs.

Updating a project

For an exact compiler pin, use this in each participating Cell.toml:

[package]
edition = "2027"
cellscript_version = "=0.33.0"

Category: Standards Track. Status: Proposal.
Abstract
This RFC defines a way to prove, off chain, that the holder of a key controls a CKB lock script, for any lock that signs the transaction hash. The prover signs a transaction that can never be committed: its only input points at an out point no transaction can create, and its only output, under the claimed lock, holds a message written by the party that asks. The verifier rebuilds that transaction from the lock and the message, resolves the input itself, and runs the lock in CKB-VM. If the lock accepts, the key controls the lock. Nothing moves on chain.
It follows BIP-322 (generic signed message format for Bitcoin) and serves the purpose EIP-1271 serves for Ethereum contract accounts.
Motivation
A service sometimes needs to know that the person behind one of its accounts controls a CKB lock. A governance site, for example, counts the Nervos DAO deposits under a lock as that account’s voting weight.
On CKB a lock is a program. A verifier that checks one signature scheme (secp256k1 with a known message prefix) cannot check a passkey lock, a multisig, an Omnilock in a foreign chain’s mode or a smart-account lock. Every wallet can already sign a transaction that spends a cell under its lock. If the proof is such a transaction, every wallet can produce one with the code it has, and one verifier, which runs the lock as the node would, handles every lock.

The key words “MUST”, “MUST NOT”, “SHOULD”, “SHOULD NOT” and “MAY” are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

Account: {account}
Lock hash: {lock hash}
Chain: {chain}
Issued at: {issued at}
Nonce: {nonce}

Format

host name of the platform, optional :port; letters, digits, . and -

1 to 256 printable ASCII characters (0x20 to 0x7e), no space at either end

A wallet that receives the transaction without the input cell MUST rebuild it from the transaction: capacity u64::MAX, the lock of the only output, no type, empty data. It MUST NOT look the input up on chain, since it does not exist.

Input: the claimed lock L, the message M, the signed transaction T, and the platform’s expectation E: the exact message it issued for this nonce, its domain, the account, the nonce, the chain’s genesis hash from its own configuration, and an age window. A node error means “could not verify”, not “refused”. Steps 1 to 7 read nothing from the chain.

Parse M. Refuse when it is not the six lines above.
Refuse unless M equals E’s message byte for byte.

Value

Platform requirements
A verifier only says that a lock accepted one transaction. A platform that counts anything from a binding MUST also:
Write the message itself, store the exact text per nonce, and compare byte for byte. It MUST NOT rebuild the message from the proof.
Issue each nonce for one account and one lock hash, and mark it used with a compare-and-set no later than the first chain read.
Take the genesis hash from its configuration, never from the message or the node.
Keep at most one active binding per lock hash. Moving a binding to another account notifies the previous one, and the moved binding counts only after a cooldown.

Wallet behaviour
A wallet SHOULD recognise a proof: a transaction equal to the proof transaction for one of its locks and the message in its only output, cell deps, header deps, since and witness aside. It SHOULD then show a sign-in request rather than a transfer: the domain next to the origin of the site that asks, with a warning when they differ, the account and the chain. It SHOULD NOT show the input’s capacity as an amount: nothing leaves the account.
Rationale
Index 0xffffffff. No transaction can have 2^32 - 1 outputs within the block size limit, so the out point cannot exist and the signed proof can never be committed.
P commits to the tag, the lock and the message. Another lock or another message gives another transaction, so a signature cannot be moved between them. The tag keeps P apart from any real transaction hash, and names the bytes being signed: a change to those bytes gets a new tag.
Input capacity u64::MAX. Some locks let a key move only a limited amount per transaction. At u64::MAX such a key sees the whole account leave and cannot prove the lock; a key with no limit can. The transaction hash covers out points, not the cells they resolve to, so this value is not part of the signed bytes for locks that sign the transaction hash.
Output under the claimed lock. Output locks never run. The output names the lock, so a wallet with several locks reads from the transaction which one is asked to sign, and a signer that gets the transaction without the input cell can rebuild it. The lock is part of the signed bytes, so a transaction whose output lock differs from the lock P commits to is a proof for no lock.
Output capacity (8 + s + n) CKB. The occupied capacity of that output. CCC 1.19 and later raises an output to its occupied capacity while building, so fixing this value makes every implementation build the same bytes.
The verifier builds the transaction. If it accepted any transaction with input 0 under L, a prover could add inputs or outputs that open L without the key: an owner-lock style lock accepts when another input carries a given lock hash, and anyone-can-pay accepts without a signature when an output under the same lock receives more than the input. With one input at u64::MAX and one output holding less, anyone-can-pay still asks for the signature.
Message shape. The first line follows EIP-4361 (Sign-In with Ethereum), so it reads the same way to users who have seen that. The account is ASCII only, so it cannot carry line breaks, direction overrides or look-alike letters into the text a wallet shows.
Rejected: a real input that cannot be spent yet
An earlier draft let wallets that only sign real inputs use a live cell of the lock with since set to a block far in the future. It was dropped: such a since satisfies time locks that have not matured, the outflow is only a fee so a key with a per-transaction limit can prove the whole account, the real input may carry a type script that opens the lock another way, and the message is only visible as a hash.
Security considerations
Cell deps come from the chain as live cells, never from the prover. A lock’s code and settings can live in deps. A forged settings cell that lists the attacker’s key would make some locks accept.
The input is a constant of the verifier, never a cell the prover names.
No exclusive control, no proof. A lock that accepts an empty witness opens for anyone. A lock that accepts the same witness on another message (a password or hash-preimage lock) lets anyone who has seen one proof make another. The two probes of step 12 refuse both kinds. A lock written to tell a probe from a real proof could still pass them.
No lock an administrator can open. An Omnilock with the administrator flag (args byte 21, bit 0) is also opened by any identity on an admin list the administrator controls. The verifier refuses such locks, for the owner’s proofs too.
Read the VM’s result, not text the script printed. A debugger that prints script logs on the same stream as its result can be fooled by a script that prints a result line.
Replay:
Replay
Stopped by
the same proof, same platform
nonce used once
a proof made for another platform
domain
another account on the same platform
account, and the stored message
another lock
the stored message, and P
testnet on mainnet, or the reverse
chain line, against the platform’s configuration and the node
an old proof
issued at window
the proof sent to the chain
its input does not exist
A proof shows control at verification time. A key can be shared later, and for locks whose code is upgradable or whose settings live in cells, the keys that control a lock can change. Requirement 5 ties a binding to the cells its proof used.
Not covered:
relative time locks, and time-dependent conditions in general: the input is fabricated, and the lock sees the since the wallet sets, not the chain’s time;
locks whose signature does not cover the transaction hash;
locks that need more than one input or one witness;
locks that read the input’s capacity and could overflow on u64::MAX;
type scripts, which are never run.
Backwards compatibility
An earlier form of this proof put the output under the lock { code_hash: 0x00 * 32, hash_type: "data", args: 0x } with capacity (41 + n) CKB and the tag CKB lock proof v0\n. It is a different transaction, a signature for one form does not open the other, and verifiers following this RFC refuse it at step 7.
Reference implementation and test vectors
ckb-ward (GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-ward: Ward: lock proof for CKB. Prove control of any CKB lock with a proof transaction that can never land on chain. · GitHub, npm ckb-ward) implements the message, the transaction, the verifier, and three runners: one built from the node’s own script crates, one on ckb-debugger, and one on ckb-vm-js in a browser. It carries 17 signed proofs, each replayed by its tests with the expected exit codes for the proof and for controls: secp256k1 (testnet and mainnet), JoyID main key (testnet and mainnet, signed in the JoyID app), JoyID sub key, a 2-of-3 multisig, anyone-can-pay, Omnilock in Dogecoin, Ethereum and Bitcoin modes, PW-lock (testnet and mainnet), the Nostr lock, the quantum-resistant lock with an SLH-DSA key (testnet and mainnet), and a smart-account lock in two configurations. The full byte-exact vectors are in its docs/SPEC.md.
CCC’s signer JSON-RPC rebuilds the input cell as described above, so a wallet connected through it can sign a proof for any of its locks. The change (ckb-devrel/ccc#641) is merged into CCC’s development branch and not yet in a release.

Rationale

  • Index 0xffffffff. No transaction can have 2^32 - 1 outputs within the block size limit, so the out point cannot exist and the signed proof can never be committed.
  • P commits to the tag, the lock and the message. Another lock or another message gives another transaction, so a signature cannot be moved between them. The tag keeps P apart from any real transaction hash, and names the bytes being signed: a change to those bytes gets a new tag.
  • Input capacity u64::MAX. Some locks let a key move only a limited amount per transaction. At u64::MAX such a key sees the whole account leave and cannot prove the lock; a key with no limit can. The transaction hash covers out points, not the cells they resolve to, so this value is not part of the signed bytes for locks that sign the transaction hash.
  • Output under the claimed lock. Output locks never run. The output names the lock, so a wallet with several locks reads from the transaction which one is asked to sign, and a signer that gets the transaction without the input cell can rebuild it. The lock is part of the signed bytes, so a transaction whose output lock differs from the lock P commits to is a proof for no lock.
  • Output capacity (8 + s + n) CKB. The occupied capacity of that output. CCC 1.19 and later raises an output to its occupied capacity while building, so fixing this value makes every implementation build the same bytes.
  • The verifier builds the transaction. If it accepted any transaction with input 0 under L, a prover could add inputs or outputs that open L without the key: an owner-lock style lock accepts when another input carries a given lock hash, and anyone-can-pay accepts without a signature when an output under the same lock receives more than the input. With one input at u64::MAX and one output holding less, anyone-can-pay still asks for the signature.
  • Message shape. The first line follows EIP-4361 (Sign-In with Ethereum), so it reads the same way to users who have seen that. The account is ASCII only, so it cannot carry line breaks, direction overrides or look-alike letters into the text a wallet shows.

Rejected: a real input that cannot be spent yet

An earlier draft let wallets that only sign real inputs use a live cell of the lock with since set to a block far in the future. It was dropped: such a since satisfies time locks that have not matured, the outflow is only a fee so a key with a per-transaction limit can prove the whole account, the real input may carry a type script that opens the lock another way, and the message is only visible as a hash.

Security considerations

  1. Cell deps come from the chain as live cells, never from the prover. A lock’s code and settings can live in deps. A forged settings cell that lists the attacker’s key would make some locks accept.
  2. The input is a constant of the verifier, never a cell the prover names.
  3. No exclusive control, no proof. A lock that accepts an empty witness opens for anyone. A lock that accepts the same witness on another message (a password or hash-preimage lock) lets anyone who has seen one proof make another. The two probes of step 12 refuse both kinds. A lock written to tell a probe from a real proof could still pass them.
  4. No lock an administrator can open. An Omnilock with the administrator flag (args byte 21, bit 0) is also opened by any identity on an admin list the administrator controls. The verifier refuses such locks, for the owner’s proofs too.
  5. Read the VM’s result, not text the script printed. A debugger that prints script logs on the same stream as its result can be fooled by a script that prints a result line.

Replay:

Replay Stopped by
the same proof, same platform nonce used once
a proof made for another platform domain
another account on the same platform account, and the stored message
another lock the stored message, and P
testnet on mainnet, or the reverse chain line, against the platform’s configuration and the node
an old proof issued at window
the proof sent to the chain its input does not exist

A proof shows control at verification time. A key can be shared later, and for locks whose code is upgradable or whose settings live in cells, the keys that control a lock can change. Requirement 5 ties a binding to the cells its proof used.

Not covered:

  • relative time locks, and time-dependent conditions in general: the input is fabricated, and the lock sees the since the wallet sets, not the chain’s time;
  • locks whose signature does not cover the transaction hash;
  • locks that need more than one input or one witness;
  • locks that read the input’s capacity and could overflow on u64::MAX;
  • type scripts, which are never run.

Backwards compatibility

An earlier form of this proof put the output under the lock { code_hash: 0x00 * 32, hash_type: "data", args: 0x } with capacity (41 + n) CKB and the tag CKB lock proof v0\n. It is a different transaction, a signature for one form does not open the other, and verifiers following this RFC refuse it at step 7.

Reference implementation and test vectors

ckb-ward (GitHub - LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-ward: Ward: lock proof for CKB. Prove control of any CKB lock with a proof transaction that can never land on chain. · GitHub, npm ckb-ward) implements the message, the transaction, the verifier, and three runners: one built from the node’s own script crates, one on ckb-debugger, and one on ckb-vm-js in a browser. It carries 17 signed proofs, each replayed by its tests with the expected exit codes for the proof and for controls: secp256k1 (testnet and mainnet), JoyID main key (testnet and mainnet, signed in the JoyID app), JoyID sub key, a 2-of-3 multisig, anyone-can-pay, Omnilock in Dogecoin, Ethereum and Bitcoin modes, PW-lock (testnet and mainnet), the Nostr lock, the quantum-resistant lock with an SLH-DSA key (testnet and mainnet), and a smart-account lock in two configurations. The full byte-exact vectors are in its docs/SPEC.md.

CCC’s signer JSON-RPC rebuilds the input cell as described above, so a wallet connected through it can sign a proof for any of its locks. The change (ckb-devrel/ccc#641) is merged into CCC’s development branch and not yet in a release.

Hi @xingtian, thanks for the feedback. I’ve revised the proposal:
Pilot outcomes: added four pre-registered hypotheses with pass/fail thresholds and a rule for continuing or stopping:
payouts happen exactly once
promoters still get paid when their browser was offline
logging a sale fits a real shop counter
promoters actually bring customers (at least 20 referred sales and 6 of 10 promoters with a sale in 14 days)
A public web demo anyone can try also goes live in week 2.
Budget: removed development time. It now lists only direct costs, $113 in total: the VPS, QR and print materials for the pilot shops, mobile data for participants, and airtime for feedback interviews. Testnet fees are $0 because test CKB comes from the faucet.
Thanks again, and happy to adjust anything else.
